units: two neighbouring dwellings show opposite characters
the older one has thick mineral walls and few openings
the newer one offers wide glazed surfaces on a light frame
the old building holds its coolness better when the air is hot
the new building follows outside temperature swings quickly

a waterproof layer was fitted under the outer cladding of the new dwelling
the halting of air renewal worries the occupants of the new dwelling
a building trade professional holds that each construction answers a distinct aim
text: Two houses stand side by side along the same road, and you tell them apart at a glance. The older one squats low: thick stone walls, a shallow roof, hardly a window anywhere. Its neighbour rises taller, with wide panes of glass set into a slender timber frame. Through the hot months the old walls hold their coolness and warm up slowly once the air turns; the newer house tracks whatever the weather does outside and answers the slightest shift. Tenants in the old one grumble about a porous render that drinks up damp rising from the ground. Those next door praise the sealed membrane laid behind their cladding, yet they dread the stale air that gathers when the ventilation stops. A builder from round here weighs up both and refuses to pick a winner: one was raised to last without fuss, the other to burn less energy.

units: the writer holds that hasty building work spoils the look of the streets
he regrets that heavy hand-worked materials are giving way to light parts
he notes the disappearance of dwellings with irregular shapes
those irregular shapes came from awkward plots or from holdings split between heirs
current buildings repeat matching volumes stacked up without hesitation
the roominess of a home was once judged by its side spaces such as lofts and cellars
it is now judged by the number of rooms advertised
the writer refuses to call for a return to the past
he asks that a building be weighed on what it will offer the following generation
text: Building in haste has become a habit, and that habit is making our streets poorer. Look at what slips away, one item at a time. Material first: the heavy block, cut by hand with a chisel, gives way to light panels which no palm has ever smoothed. Shape next: the crooked dwelling, born of an awkward plot or of a holding split between heirs, vanishes in favour of matching volumes stacked up without a pause for thought. Use last of all: a roomy home was once judged by its lofts and its cellars, by everything tucked around the edges; now it is judged by the number of rooms printed in a listing. I plead for no return to any earlier age, and I distrust easy longing. I ask only that a building be weighed on what it will offer the generation after us, not on the speed of its site.

he teaches that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan received from afar
text: The carpenter started out as an apprentice on a refurbishment site, where sorting the beams fell to him. He had to tell rough but sound timber from a crumbling length eaten away by damp. After three seasons he moved to a workshop that cut its joints by hand, using neither glue nor metal fixings. There he learnt setting out, full-scale drawing, the angled cut, and then fitting onto walls that never stood quite true. A fall from scaffolding kept him off site through a long recovery; he filled those months drawing roof frames for other teams. On his return he opened up a workshop of his own and took on two apprentices. He tells them over and over again that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan arriving by post, because an old wall shifts and no frontage is ever straight.

text: What this refurbishment deserves credit for is chiefly what it avoided. Cracks ran through the building from the ground to the ridge, because a broken gutter had soaked the foundations over a very long stretch of time. The water working in dissolved the mortar, the stones slid out of line, and the staircase lost its footing. The site manager therefore dealt with the origin of the trouble before its appearance: he drained the foot of the wall, made the bonding good again, and replaced the worn treads. That ordering of priorities explains how solid the work now stands. It explains too how quiet the result looks, which some visitors find disappointing for want of any visible effect. The windows are too uniform, and they rub out the trace of the older openings. The choice holds up all the same: ornament laid over unsteady walls would have split apart.

the joiner put a stout prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again

the neighbour and the writer made their peace after that repair
text: I have a spare moment, so let me tell you how the floor saga ended. Ever since I moved into this flat above an old workshop, every step set the boards creaking and woke the woman living underneath. I tried packing pieces, screws, thick rugs, and none of it made the slightest difference. Then a joiner came round to have a look and found the cause in one visit. The joists were resting on a beam that had sagged, and the hollow beneath the floor made every footfall boom. He put a stout prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again onto fresh battens. The quiet came back that very evening. My neighbour brought me a potted plant to mark the news, and we laughed about two miserable seasons spent blaming each other. Come and see me soon, the spare room is ready and waiting for you.

units: heating costs depend on what the walls are made of and not on the age of the building
a thick wall stores heat and gives it back overnight
a lightweight partition loses its heat as soon as the heating stops
insulation works differently on an old wall and on a recent one
an old wall must let vapour through, otherwise water builds up inside its thickness
a recent wall calls for an unbroken barrier and for controlled air renewal
builders advise choosing what you can mend yourself
render is made good with a bricklayer's tool
a factory-made panel has to be replaced whole
text: Does an old house cost more to heat than a newly built one? Well, it comes down to the walls, not to the age of the place. A thick wall soaks up heat and gives it back overnight, while a lightweight partition lets it go the moment the boiler cuts out. So what does insulation change? A great deal, though not in quite the same way on either side. On an old wall you have to let vapour pass through; otherwise water builds up inside the thickness and the wall slowly breaks down. On a recent one you want the opposite: an unbroken barrier, plus ventilation that carries the stale air away. Which should you go for, then? The one you can mend yourself, say the builders working round here. Render can be made good with a trowel; a factory-bonded panel is swapped whole or not at all.

text: The site manager laid out the refurbishment scheme for the neighbours who had come along to hear him, and he grouped his answers around three worries. Noise came first: knocking out the partitions would take a fortnight, he said, and the loud machinery would stand idle from late afternoon on. Dust came next: a fine sheet will wrap the scaffolding, and a spray will damp the rubble down before it is carted out. Access came last: the pavement will be diverted, though the shop on the ground floor keeps its own door. One woman asked what would become of the wall she shares with her yard; the engineer there replied that it would be propped, then repointed, at the contractor's expense. A father raised the matter of the lorries coming through at the hour when children walk home.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: lasting homes appear once groups stop moving about

the moulded block could be made again exactly alike

text: Homes meant to last appear once groups stop moving about and choose to keep their stores in one place. The earliest walls are branches daubed with mud, thrown up quickly and patched after every downpour. Then comes the finding that changes everything: silt paste dried in the sun holds far better than fresh daub, and a moulded block can be made again and again, always alike. A wall turns into a sum of like parts, and that reshapes the builder's trade as much as it reshapes the house. Later, firing in a kiln yields a reddened block that shrugs off the rain, and builders grow bold enough to pile one storey on another. The arch, and after it the vault, free openings at last from heavy timber crossbeams. Every step forward rested on a repeated gesture and on a material taking over from the one before.

units: an inside wall can turn damp with no leak at all
the air of a heated home carries vapour from cooking, showering and breathing
the vapour turns into droplets when it meets a cold surface
chilled air holds less water than warm air

the surface finish soaked with water ends up covered in dark patches

carrying the vapour away with steady ventilation also removes the cause
drying the patch alone settles nothing, since the cold surface remains
text: An inside wall can turn damp with no leak anywhere, and the physics behind it is plain enough. The air of a heated home carries vapour, given off by cooking, by showering, and by the breathing of the people who live there. That vapour drifts about freely until it meets a cold surface. There it turns into droplets, because chilled air holds less water than warm air does. The cold spot usually comes from a local gap in the insulation: a concrete lintel, a poorly protected corner, a window sill running right through the wall. Condensation settles, the surface finish grows sodden, and dark patches begin to spread. Two remedies act on the cause: warm the surface by putting the fault right, or carry the vapour away with steady ventilation. Drying the patch alone changes nothing, since the cold surface is still there.

the rules of the building now call for an examination of the structure before any covering is stripped
text: A housing block of three buildings ran into an instructive mishap while its roof was being redone. The firm engaged had stripped the covering off a whole wing before checking the frame beneath, and the inspection turned up worm-eaten rafters along the entire length. Work stopped, the temporary sheeting gave way under a downpour, and water ruined the ceilings on the top floor. The residents met and refused to settle a second estimate. A mediator put a way out to them: the firm would redo the ceilings at its own cost, and the owners would fund the replacement timber, which nobody could have foreseen in so old a structure. The agreement held. The lesson now sits in the rules of the building: no covering is to be stripped before the structure it shelters has been fully examined.
